examples: An international conference on environmental issues was held.
The family dispute over the inheritance has dragged on.
Rumors within the company about personnel matters never stop.
Public opinion on education reform is split in two.
The debate between the ruling and opposition parties over national security continued.
Differences in the interpretation of historical facts have come to the surface.
fields.explain:
Placed right before the head noun to sum up the content "surrounding N".
Formal and concise; favored in administrative documents, journalism, and academic writing.
Suitable when you want to emphasize multiple sides or a conflict of interests/opinions.
Not used as a predicate: ×「この問題をめぐる。」→ you must write 「この問題をめぐって議論している。」

• Modifies the following noun, meaning "related to / surrounding (the issue N)" with a nuance of controversy, opposition, multiple parties.
• Creates concise noun phrases suited to titles and headlines: ～をめぐる論争／～をめぐる対立／～をめぐる疑惑.
• Scope of use: politics, society, economics, law, academia, organizations.
fields.notes:
• Contracted form for headlines: 「Nをめぐる混乱」「Nをめぐる疑惑」 keeps the sentence short and informative.
• Several modifiers can be stacked: 「資源開発をめぐる国際的な政治的対立」, but use restraint so it does not become hard to read.
• Often used with adjectives: 深刻な/複雑な/激しい + NをめぐるN.
mistakes: Using ～をめぐる as a predicate: ×「問題をめぐる。」→ grammatically incorrect.
Confusing it with ～についてのN: JLPT questions test the nuance of "controversy/opposition". If there are keywords like 対立/論争/賛否 → choose ～をめぐる.
Using it for small, personal topics → sounds exaggerated and unnatural.
Missing the noun after ～をめぐる: there must always be an N right after it (mandatory modifier).

fields.connection: いつまで + V plain form + のやら
examples: I wonder how long this recession will last.
I wonder how long I'm supposed to wait. No word has come.
I wonder how long I'll have to put up with this.
Who knows how long prices will keep rising. There's no end in sight.
I wonder how long that child will be in this rebellious phase.
fields.explain:
Used when the speaker wonders to themselves about something hard to predict, with emotion attached.
Not used to question the person you are talking to; for a real question, use いつまで～か／いつまで～のですか .
Placed at the end of a sentence; the plain form comes before のやら. With na-adjectives/N, use なのやら .

いつまで～のやら expresses a feeling of uncertainty, worry, or lament: "I wonder how long…". It is a rhetorical question that does not require an answer.
• Nuance: emotion (worry, lament, weariness, helplessness), leaning toward monologue.
• Often used in light written language, diaries, and monologues; rarely used to ask other people directly.
• The sentence can end with a period or a question mark depending on style; grammatically it is a rhetorical question.
fields.notes:
• のやら is more literary than のかな; it fits narration of a character's state of mind.
• Modal words can be inserted before のやら: 一体／果たして／全く to emphasize bewilderment.
• With なのやら, don't forget the な for na-adjectives/nouns.
mistakes: Using です/ます right before のやら is incorrect: say 高いのやら, not 高いですのやら.
Using it to question other people sounds rude; the JLPT often tests distinguishing it from ～か/～のですか.
Confusing it with the listing pattern ～やら～やら (a completely different function).

fields.connection: どうにか(して) + V potential form ない + ものか
examples: Isn't there something that can be done about this traffic jam?
The budget is tight, but isn't there some way to at least not lower the quality?
Couldn't we somehow get the department manager to make some time for us?
I wonder if this problem couldn't somehow be solved with the help of experts.
There are far too many accidents. Can't the countermeasures somehow be sped up?
fields.explain:
Used when the speaker feels pressed and wants to change a bad situation; usually a shared or work-related problem.
More formal with ないものだろうか; blunt and somewhat harsh with ないものか.
Often combined with degree words such as "どうにか/なんとか/せめて". "どうにか" is neutral; "なんとか" is more colloquial.
The one carrying out the action is usually not just the speaker; it implies the need to "find a way".
Not used for small direct requests; used for things that are difficult or have been tried without success.

- Expresses a strong desire: "Isn't there (some way) to…?", "Is there any way to…?". Often used when the matter is difficult or beyond the speaker's control.
- The nuance is complaint/regret + hope of finding a solution. The degree of longing is higher than ordinary patterns for asking opinions.
- Used with: verbs in the potential form (できる/られる), or てもらう (hoping to have someone else do it). The fixed phrase どうにかならないものか emphasizes "isn't there any way to manage?".
- "ものか" here is a particle that emphasizes a rhetorical question; it can be replaced by "ものだろうか" to soften the frustration.
fields.notes:
- "どうにか" and "なんとか" are mostly interchangeable; "どうにか" sounds neutral/written, "なんとか" is colloquial and more emotional.
- Polite/written forms: ～ないものだろうか ＞ ～ないだろうか ＞ ～ないものか (strong). Choose according to the relationship and context.
- せめて can be added to narrow the scope of the wish: せめて納期だけでも守れないものだろうか。
mistakes: Using it for easy/trivial matters → sounds too serious. Use ～てくれない？ instead of ～ないものか.
Confusing the agent: this pattern does not emphasize "I will do it" but "there is a way/someone/some condition to…".
Dropping the "potential" of the verb: prefer V-られない/できない. Example: ×増やさないものか → better: 増やせないものか.
Confusing it with a simple negative: ～ないものか is a question expressing desire, not a statement that "it is not…".
In exams, the polite answer is usually ～ないものだろうか in formal contexts (official documents, proposals).

fields.meaning:
～だけ（書(か)き言葉(ことば)）
Only
examples: Only one slot per prefecture is allowed to compete in the national baseball tournament.
All I can do now is pray that my father is safe.
A leader must not be merely strict. Otherwise, young people won't follow.
Recently, more universities are holding interviews, not just paper tests.
Not only did he kill someone, he also tried to pin the crime on someone else.
* To pass the T University entrance exam, all it takes is hard work!

fields.meaning: If (by any chance)… then… (serious consequences will follow)
examples: If there's even the slightest sound outside, our dog barks furiously.

A: This report is tough, isn't it? I'm tempted to just borrow someone's paper from the internet.
B: I know how you feel. But if you did something like that, you'd definitely not get the credits.
fields.notes: A somewhat exaggerated way of stating a condition, expressing the meaning "if by any chance such a thing were to happen." It is normally followed by content saying that "a serious situation will arise." (５９８)

fields.meaning:
Let's… together! (a call to action, rallying; formal) | 一緒(いっしょ)に～しよう（他社(たしゃ)への呼(よ)びかけ）
Do… together
examples: We've come all this way, so why don't we enjoy ourselves to the fullest?
＜Written text＞Everyone has their own worries. But just thinking about them won't solve them. Even if it is hard, let us move forward one step at a time.
fields.notes:
explain: Expresses a strong call to action or a strong will; often used by men.
Formal sentence style.
⏐ examples: 1. 今日はお祝いだ。みんなで飲もうではないか。
Today is a celebration. Let's all drink together!
2. だれもやらないなら、ぼくがやってみようじゃないか。
If nobody else will do it, then I'll give it a try myself.

examples: He's bad at Japanese. On top of that, he can't speak English either.
This shop is expensive. On top of that, the service is bad too.
It's been raining since this morning. And to top it off, I forgot my umbrella.
He's slow at work. On top of that, he makes lots of mistakes.
I have a cold. And on top of that, I've even started running a fever.
fields.explain:
Position : At the beginning of clause B, following a complete sentence or clause A.
Nuance : Carries strong emotion, usually dissatisfaction or complaint; but it can also be used in a positive sense.
Style : Casual, colloquial; rarely used in formal written language or theses.
When used in a positive sense, the nuance is cheerful and humorous:彼は優しい。 おまけに、ハンサムだ。

•
Expresses addition: B is additional information to A, making the situation better or (usually) worse.

•
Emotional nuance: Often used when the speaker wants to complain, reproach, or emphasize that something is "unlucky, annoying, piling on".

•
Equivalent meaning in English: "On top of that…", "In addition…", "And that's not all…".

• Rarely used in formal writing; mainly appears in conversation, spoken language, stories, and casual writing.
fields.notes:
• Often used when listing successive unfavorable conditions to create a "one bad thing after another" effect.
• In casual conversation, it can be replaced by "しかもさ" or "それにしてもさ" depending on the degree of emotion.
• Positive uses also occur but are rarer and have a playful nuance. explain: Used in spoken language. A word more commonly used in speech than 「しかも」 ⏐ examples: 1. 日本の夏は暑いし、おまけに湿気も多いです。
Summers in Japan are hot, and on top of that, very humid.
2. あのそば屋は高いしまずい。おまけにサービスも悪い。
That soba shop is expensive and the food is bad. On top of that, the service is poor.
mistakes: Confusing it with それに: それに is neutral, whereas おまけに carries a strong emotional nuance.
Using it in formal writing → inappropriate; use その上 or さらに instead.
Using it when A and B do not point in the same direction → illogical (おまけに is used when B adds information in the same direction as A).
Omitting the comma in written language: you should write "おまけに、～"。

examples: This computer is light. What's more, the battery lasts a long time.
He is young. Moreover, he has a wealth of experience.
There's a traffic jam. On top of that, there's even been an accident.
The food at this restaurant is good. What's more, the prices are reasonable.
The rain is heavy. What's more, the wind speed keeps rising.
fields.explain:
Used when you want to emphasize that the additional information is "significant/surprising".
Suitable for argumentative writing, presentations, and advertising.
Placed at the beginning of the sentence S2; it can also be placed mid-sentence to connect two attributes of the same subject.
Avoid using it to introduce a request/command; it sounds forced.
Often used together with まで・さえ to widen the scope.

しかも: "moreover, besides, on top of that"; emphasizes that S2 is an additional element that is surprising/noteworthy, raising the evaluation in the same direction as S1.
• Intensifying effect: S2 makes the impression stronger (better or worse).
• Style: neutral to formal; can be used in reports/articles.
• Does not express a cause-and-effect relationship; it is only emphatic addition.
fields.notes:
• In rhetoric, the sequence "まず… 次に… しかも…" creates a sense of escalating argument.
• "しかも" can follow a semicolon or comma in literary writing for a stronger rhythm.
• Tip: if you want to sound more "persuasive" than それに, choose しかも. explain: Used when adding another thing or matter to a certain thing or matter. ⏐ examples: 1. 彼女は美人で頭がいい。しかも性格もいい。
She is beautiful and smart. What's more, she has a good personality.
2. 先日泊まったホテルは、古くて高かった。しかもサービスが悪かったので、もう二度と行かない。
The hotel I stayed at the other day was old and expensive. What's more, the service was bad, so I'm never going there again.
mistakes: Using it for a cause-and-effect relationship: ×「雨だ。しかも、試合を中止した」→ use それで/したがって instead.
Mixing it up with そのうえ/それに: questions asking you to choose a conjunction require a degree of emphasis ⇒ しかも is the answer when S2 is "more striking".
Using it with a command/suggestion sounds forced: ×「しかも、来てください」.
The direction of evaluation must be consistent (positive + positive or negative + negative) to be natural.

examples: A typhoon is approaching. Therefore, today's event is canceled.
Costs have risen. Therefore, a price revision is necessary.
The evidence is insufficient. Therefore, it cannot be said that the defendant is guilty.
Demand has expanded rapidly. Therefore, we will consider increasing production.
This equipment has become old and worn. Therefore, we recommend replacing it.
fields.explain:
Formal style; suitable for reports, announcements, and academic presentations.
Position: at the beginning of the sentence stating the conclusion; usually followed by a comma.
Should not be used before personal, direct commands/requests.
Often appears in argument sequences: まず/第一に →次に → したがって /結論.

したがって: "therefore/so/accordingly". States a conclusion or inevitable consequence based on the premise just mentioned. Often used in academic texts, reports, and official announcements.
• Highly logical, with little emotional nuance.
• S2 is usually a judgment, conclusion, policy, or objective resulting state.
• Unnatural when followed by a personal request or a direct command.
fields.notes:
• Distinguish "従って" (conjunction: therefore) from "規則に従って" (meaning "in accordance with"). They look the same but function differently.
• In formal speeches there is a keigo variant "したがいまして" (rarely used in standard writing, but heard in ceremonial speech).
• Tip: if the sentence is a conclusion about a policy/regulation, したがって is usually a good choice. explain: Expresses that the following matter occurs as a natural result of the conditions in the preceding sentence.
Used in formal sentences. ⏐ examples: 1. 彼はまじめて誠実な人だ。したがってみんなから信頼されている。
He is a serious and sincere person. Therefore, he is trusted by everyone.
2. 教授は急用で来られません。したがって講義は中止です。
The professor cannot come due to urgent business. Therefore, the lecture is canceled.
mistakes: Using it before a personal request: ×「したがって、来てください」→ use ですので/それで instead.
Confusing it with そのため/それで: for sentences with academic, logical reasoning → したがって; for everyday sentences with a natural result → それで.
Mixing it up with the meaning "in accordance with": check whether an object + に comes before it (規則に従って = a different pattern from the conjunction).

rows: <ruby>熱<rt>ねつ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>た。それで、<ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>んだ。
Written language; emphasizes the reason rather than a logical conclusion.
<ruby>渋滞<rt>じゅうたい</rt></ruby>。そのため、<ruby>遅刻<rt>ちこく</rt></ruby>した。
Very academic/literary; stronger than したがって.
<ruby>証拠<rt>しょうこ</rt></ruby><ruby>不十分<rt>ふじゅうぶん</rt></ruby>、ゆえに<ruby>無罪<rt>むざい</rt></ruby>。

examples: The room was cold. So I turned on the heater.
The bus didn't come. So I decided to take a taxi.
The report deadline is close. So I plan to stay up all night tonight.
My computer broke. So I decided to buy a new one.
This problem is difficult. So let's try asking the teacher.
fields.explain:
Position : Always at the beginning of the second clause, after a period or comma.
Suitable context : When B is an intentional action to resolve the situation in A.
Style : Reasoned and logical – often used in writing, storytelling, and reports.
Nuance : Polite and neutral; not as colloquial as それでさ, nor as formal as従って.

•
Expresses an action/solution based on the preceding situation: A is the circumstance or problem → B is the action taken to deal with or respond to it.

•
Natural translations: "So…", "Therefore…", "That's why…".

•
Emphasizes reasonableness and the speaker's deliberate conclusion: Unlike "そして", which just connects, "そこで" shows a shift to action.

•
Often used in storytelling, reports, and descriptions of how a problem was solved.
fields.notes:
• Often appears in JLPT reading comprehension when explaining a solution or the steps for dealing with a problem.
• Often used in logical presentations, scientific reports, and talks: problem → solution.
• Not used when B is an emotion or an unexpected result (use すると in that case). explain: Used when developing a story. A conjunction indicating that the following sentence presents a way of solving, a suggestion, or a request. ⏐ examples: 1. 明日は車が混むらしい。そこで我々は朝早く出発するつもりだ。
I hear the roads will be crowded tomorrow. So we plan to leave early in the morning.
2. 「今度アメリカに旅行します。そこでお願いがあるのですが．．．。」
I'm going on a trip to America soon. So I have a favor to ask…
mistakes: Confusing it with それで: それで only states a natural result; そこで emphasizes an intentional action.
Using it for an unexpected result: Incorrect. In this case, use すると.
Illogical when A is not a problem/situation: そこで requires A to provide a reason for carrying out B.
Omitting the comma after そこで in formal written language → you should write: "そこで、…"。

rows: Emphasizes an action to solve the problem.
<ruby>寒<rt>さむ</rt></ruby>い。 そこでコートを<ruby>着<rt>き</rt></ruby>た。
<ruby>寒<rt>さむ</rt></ruby>い。 それで<ruby>風邪<rt>かぜ</rt></ruby>をひいた。
<ruby>寒<rt>さむ</rt></ruby>い。 だから<ruby>嫌<rt>いや</rt></ruby>なんだ。
The result happens immediately, often unexpectedly.
ドアを<ruby>開<rt>あ</rt></ruby>けた。 すると<ruby>猫<rt>ねこ</rt></ruby>がいた。
